candidates.title: VEPA: Verified Evolving Formal Policy for Lifelong LLM Agent Guardrails
candidates.citationVelocity: published 5 days (submitted 2026-10-08); Semantic Scholar confirms 0 citations
candidates.institution: Google Cloud AI Research / Google DeepMind / University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill
communitySignals: no reproduction repo found on Papers with Code
credibilityEvidence: Section 4.2 (RQ1): F1 0.81/0.76 on ASSEBench-Safety/ATBench final round, 0.02/0.09 above strongest baseline, with active-policy coverage reaching ~80/89/88%
Section 4.3 (RQ2): mixed-stream F1≈0.86 vs AGrail 0.78/LiSA 0.80; noisy-feedback (10% label flip) F1≈0.81 vs 0.77/0.76
Section 5: ablation study, long-horizon deployment, and generalization across LLM backbones reported separately
Appendix D: formal derivation of the guarantee boundary (structural invariants, evidence-aware authority criterion)
candidates.evidenceMaturityReason: Covers reliability/scope of formal authority, three types of adverse deployment conditions (mixed streams, noisy feedback, long horizons), ablations, and cross-backbone generalization, each with reported numbers
reproducibilityEvidence: Method, baselines, hyperparameters, and prompts detailed in Appendices B and G; no public code or dataset repository link found in the paper
candidates.editorialConfidenceReason: The claim is explicitly bounded to 'guarantees apply after parsing' and the paper's own Limitations section (Appendix F) names this exact boundary, matching the strength of the claim used in the article
candidates.primaryLimitation: Formal guarantees only hold after an agent event has been correctly parsed into the typed DSL by a neural (LLM) parser; parser errors or adversarial inputs fall outside the guarantee boundary, and the current policy language is limited to binary allow/refuse over a fixed schema
candidates.presentationReason: Problem formulation (conflict/regression definitions), method (two-layer generation/verification/authority), and limitations are stated precisely with formal definitions
candidates.reason: First to combine deterministic, auditable formal-policy enforcement with continual evolution from deployment feedback, backed by top-tier institutional authorship and robustness results across three benchmarks and five deployment conditions

candidates.title: Reward Hacking as a Transmissible Strategy in Multi-Agent Coding Systems
candidates.citationVelocity: published 5 days (submitted 2026-10-09); Semantic Scholar confirms 0 citations
communitySignals: no reproduction repo found on Papers with Code
credibilityEvidence: Section 3.2: formal reward-hacking criterion RH(s,C) combining static mechanism detection with a strict/leaky evaluator disagreement check, validated by manual label audit (Appendix B)
Sections 5-6: direct one-hop, transmission-chain, feedback-driven, shared-memory, and role-transfer propagation experiments across 4 open-weight source backbones and 14 target models
Theorem 5.1 and Appendix L: theoretical derivation of the propagation factor R=k*theta1/u0 with conditions for amplification/decay/persistence
Section 7: orchestrator-routing and candidate-aggregation experiments showing system-level effects
Section 8: two mitigation experiments (self-review, independent verifier) with quantified trade-offs
candidates.evidenceMaturityReason: Covers elicitation, four distinct propagation paths, system-level coordination effects, and two mitigations, each backed by experiments and matched to a theoretical model
reproducibilityEvidence: Detection criterion, prompts, and full experimental protocols detailed across Appendices B-S; no public code or dataset repository link found in the paper
candidates.editorialConfidenceReason: Appendix A (Discussion and Limitations) explicitly scopes the claim to Python coding tasks and three known pytest-level mechanisms, matching the bounded claim used in the article
candidates.primaryLimitation: Experiments are confined to Python coding tasks and three known pytest-level hacking mechanisms; propagation strength is highly model-dependent (GPT-5.5 showed near-zero susceptibility), and mitigation experiments focus only on the planner-to-coder setting
candidates.presentationReason: Problem formulation, propagation protocols, and limitations are stated explicitly with a dedicated Discussion and Limitations appendix
candidates.reason: First to reframe reward hacking as a system-level, transmissible failure in multi-agent coding systems rather than an individual training flaw, with rigorous cross-model propagation experiments and a matching theoretical model, from a top-tier industry/academic pairing

candidates.title: DRYLAB-Bench: Benchmarking the Biosecurity Risk of Agentic LLM Mutation Design
candidates.citationVelocity: published 4 days (submitted 2026-10-09); Semantic Scholar confirms 0 citations
candidates.institution: Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory / Fudan University
credibilityEvidence: Section 4: 15 frontier models, 30 hazardous mutation-design scenarios, scored against 187,695 real DMS measurements from ProteinGym/ViroGym via the proposed Biosecurity Risk Score (BRS)

Section 4.3 finding 1-3: baseline threat quantification (S0 BRS=0.359), tool-amplification dynamics (S1/S2 deltas with Pearson correlation analysis), and a refusal-vs-harm correlation analysis (Spearman rho=+0.25) with a controlled 'academic wrap' rewording experiment
Appendix F.2: explicit memorization-vs-genuine-capability analysis ruling out 'models just recite known answers' as the explanation
Appendix F.1: Ethics Statement and explicit scope-limiting argument for why single-site substitution is the correct evaluation unit
candidates.evidenceMaturityReason: Covers 15 models x 30 scenarios x 3 progressive tool-access settings, with ablations (S0-iter control), correlation analysis, and a dedicated memorization check
reproducibilityEvidence: Benchmark code publicly released on GitHub; however the underlying 187,695 DMS ground-truth labels are drawn from existing third-party public databases (ProteinGym/ViroGym) rather than an exclusive release of this paper
candidates.editorialConfidenceReason: Appendix F.1 explicitly bounds the claim to single-site substitution risk and states what BRS does NOT measure (multi-mutation interaction, host expression, transmissibility, in-vivo behavior), matching the claim strength used in the article
candidates.primaryLimitation: As stated by the authors: BRS does not estimate multi-mutant fitness, epistasis, host-context expression, transmissibility, or the success of a physical construction pipeline, and makes no claim about behavior in a living organism; the single-mutation scope is a deliberate, acknowledged restriction
candidates.presentationReason: Benchmark construction, metric definition, and the scope of what the metric does and does not measure are stated with unusual explicitness, including a dedicated justification section
candidates.reason: First benchmark to quantify a long-discussed but previously unmeasured dual-use biosecurity risk using a safe, scalable, large-scale empirical verification method, and the keyword-vs-intent refusal gap it surfaces has direct, immediate relevance to safety-alignment practice
